strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: adapting large vision-language models (CLIP) under personalized federated learning with heterogeneous (label/feature/domain shift) client data.

The proposed asymmetric optimization design (modality-specific up/down projections trained locally, shared cross-modal projection aggregated globally) is clean, intuitive, and offers a natural communication-efficiency benefit since only the shared component is transmitted.

Evaluation breadth is a plus: eleven datasets spanning base-to-novel class generalization, domain shift (DomainNet, Office-Caltech10), and large-scale personalization (100 clients on CIFAR-10/100), with three random seeds and reasonable baseline selection of recent federated prompt-tuning methods (PromptFL, FedPGP, FedOTP, pFedMoAP).

Results on novel-class accuracy and on the combined feature+label shift setting (Table 2) show meaningful gains over prompt-based baselines, supporting the claim of better generalization-personalization trade-off.
The paper is generally well-written and clearly structured, with a thorough related-work section covering PFL, federated prompt learning, and PEFT.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the adapter architecture is essentially adopted as-is from MMA [38], and the asymmetric aggregation is a standard partial-personalization technique (cf. FedPer, PartialFed, FedBABU, FedPerFix, FedTP). The main contribution is the combination of existing components; the paper would benefit from deeper methodological innovation or analysis explaining why the shared projection specifically drives generalization.

No ablation studies are presented in the main text: no experiments isolating the contribution of the shared projection vs. purely local adapters, no sensitivity analysis of the bottleneck dimension, scaling factor, insertion layer ℓ, or number of adapter layers. Given that the design is the core contribution, this is a significant gap.

Missing important baselines: all five baselines are prompt-based. There are no adapter- or LoRA-based federated baselines (e.g., FedPEFT/FedPETuning-style approaches, federated LoRA), which is critical given the paper's central claim that adapters outperform prompts for PFL of VLMs.

The communication-efficiency claim is only qualitative. No quantitative comparison of communicated parameters per round versus PromptFL or federated LoRA is provided, and it is unclear whether the shared projection is actually smaller than a prompt or LoRA update.

Results are mixed and the improvement on the flagship benchmark is marginal: on the 7-dataset average (Table 1), the HM improvement over PromptFL is only ~0.7 points (82.85 vs 82.15), and pFedMMA is clearly behind on several datasets (e.g., DTD HM 64.32 vs 66.75 for FedPGP; Caltech101 97.07 vs 95.70 is a win but DSLR/Webcam in Table 2 are notably worse than pFedMoAP). No statistical significance tests are reported despite the small margins.

Internal inconsistencies: the setup section (page 9) states N=12 for DomainNet and N=8 for Office-Caltech10, but Section 5.2 states 8 clients for DomainNet and 12 for Office-Caltech10; the dataset count is stated as 'nine public benchmark datasets' in one place and 'eleven datasets' in the abstract; the 'Average on 7 datasets' is unexplained given the claimed dataset count. These errors undermine confidence in experimental bookkeeping.

Under severe non-overlapping class splits, pFedMMA sacrifices substantial local accuracy (94.00 vs 97.90 for pFedMoAP) — a trade-off that deserves explicit discussion, especially for a 'personalized' FL method.
Reproducibility concerns: key details (insertion layer ℓ, hyperparameter search protocol, appendix contents, code availability) are deferred or missing; no released code is mentioned.

The paper reads as a preprint-style manuscript (18 pages, extensive preliminaries restating known PEFT/FL background) rather than a conference paper; Sections 3.2-3.3 mostly re-describe CLIP and adapters from prior work and dilute the contribution.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the proposed framework (shared cross-modal projection aggregated globally, modality-specific up/down projections kept local) is simple and easy to follow.

The evaluation covers a relatively broad set of benchmarks (CLIP datasets, DomainNet, Office-Caltech10, CIFAR-10/100) under both label shift and feature/domain shift scenarios, with base-to-novel generalization metrics.

The asymmetric aggregation idea yields a communication-efficient design, and the empirical results show a reasonable balance between personalization and generalization compared to federated prompt tuning baselines.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core method is essentially the well-known shared/private parameter decomposition strategy in PFL (e.g., FedPer, PartialFed, LG-FedAvg) applied to the existing MMA adapter architecture [38]. The 'first adapter-based approach for PFL of VLMs' claim is also questionable given FedCLIP [68] already integrates adapters in federated CLIP adaptation.

No ablation studies are presented in the main text. Crucial design choices — which layer ℓ to start inserting adapters, the bottleneck dimension, which component to share, and whether the gains come from the multi-modal design or simply from partial aggregation — are not analyzed.

The baseline comparison is incomplete and potentially unfair. All baselines are prompt-based; no adapter-based or LoRA-based federated baselines are included. FedOTP's near-collapsed base/novel accuracies (e.g., 17.99/36.69) suggest possible under-tuning of competitors, and no hyperparameter tuning protocol for baselines is described.

Internal inconsistencies undermine credibility: the abstract claims experiments on 'eleven datasets', Section 5.1 says 'nine', and Table 1 reports '7 datasets'; the client counts for DomainNet and Office-Caltech10 are stated as N=12 and N=8 in Section 5.1 but reversed in Section 5.2.

Table 2 results are unstable: pFedMMA loses substantially to baselines on several domains (e.g., Painting 16.94 vs 33.52, Webcam 15.00 vs 23.68) yet no standard deviations or significance tests are reported anywhere, and Table 2 appears to be a single-seed result.

The central claim that sharing only the middle projection improves generalization is asserted but never analyzed. There is no theoretical support, no analysis of the resulting optimization dynamics, and no quantitative measurement of the claimed communication savings (parameter counts, bytes communicated).

Gains over strong baselines are modest on local/personalized accuracy (pFedMMA is consistently behind FedPGP, FedOTP, and pFedMoAP on local classes), so the overall advantage rests heavily on the HM metric choice.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, and several important details (adapter insertion layers ℓ per backbone, appendix hyperparameters) are deferred to an appendix that is not available in the submission.
Writing quality issues (e.g., 'Implimentation Details', 'with with', 'multi-model federated frameworks') indicate insufficient polish.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant gap: adapter-based personalized federated learning for VLMs has indeed received much less attention than prompt-based approaches, and the claim of being 'the first adapter-based approach for PFL of VLMs' is plausible based on the related work survey.

The experimental coverage is broad: eleven datasets spanning label shift (pathological non-IID CLIP datasets), feature/domain shift (DomainNet, Office-Caltech10), and Dirichlet-based personalization (CIFAR-10/100 with 100 clients), with two backbone architectures and multiple seeds.

The asymmetric aggregation design (local up/down projections, globally aggregated shared projection) is sensible, communication-efficient, and clearly described with a well-structured Figure 1 and formalized update rules.

Results show a genuinely better personalization-generalization trade-off than strong recent baselines (PromptFL, FedPGP, FedOTP, pFedMoAP), particularly on novel-class accuracy, which is the claimed key advantage over prompt-based PFL.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the adapter architecture is directly taken from MMA [38], and the asymmetric shared/personalized parameter decomposition is a well-established PFL idea (FedPer, PartialFed, FedRep, parameter decomposition in [47-49]). The contribution is essentially a combination of known components; the paper should more explicitly differentiate its design decisions from prior partial-personalization work.

Missing critical baselines: all five baselines are prompt-based. There is no federated adapter/LoRA baseline (e.g., FedPETuning-style FedAvg over adapters, or a naive 'aggregate everything' adapter baseline), which is essential to isolate the benefit of the asymmetric aggregation scheme itself rather than of adapters vs. prompts.

No ablation studies in the main text. Key design choices—bottleneck dimension (32), scaling factor (0.001), which layer to start adapter insertion (ℓ), and, most importantly, which components to share (e.g., sharing the down-projection instead, or aggregating all layers)—are not ablated, so the source of the gains is unclear.

Inconsistencies that undermine confidence: the abstract claims 'eleven datasets' while Section 5.1 says 'nine public benchmark datasets' and Table 1 reports '7 datasets'; the client counts for DomainNet and Office-Caltech10 are swapped between Section 5.1 (N=12 DomainNet, N=8 Office-Caltech) and Section 5.2 (8 clients DomainNet, 12 clients Office-Caltech).

On DomainNet (Table 2), pFedMMA actually loses to baselines on several domains (Painting, Amazon, DSLR, Webcam), and the overall improvement over FedPGP (23.49 -> 31.49) is driven largely by Quickdraw and Real; per-domain analysis and variance reporting would strengthen the claim of robust superiority.

The claimed mechanisms are not analyzed: there is no empirical evidence (e.g., embedding alignment visualization, representation analysis) that the shared projection specifically is responsible for cross-modal alignment and generalization, versus simply regularizing adapters.

Parameter/memory/communication cost is claimed as a benefit but never quantified: adapters typically have far more trainable parameters than prompts, so the comparison with prompt-based methods on communication and compute budgets is incomplete.

No theoretical grounding, no code release or reproducibility statement, and no discussion of limitations or privacy considerations (sharing adapter projections can still leak client information, which is relevant given the paper's privacy motivation).

strengths: Addresses a relevant and timely problem: combining personalized federated learning with parameter-efficient adaptation of vision-language models, and clearly motivates the personalization–generalization trade-off with supporting evidence (Fig. 1).

Extensive empirical evaluation: eleven datasets covering label shift (pathological non-IID CLIP datasets), feature/label shift (DomainNet, Office-Caltech10), and Dirichlet-based personalization (CIFAR-10/100), with multiple shot settings (1-16), two backbones, and reasonably strong baselines (PromptFL, FedPGP, FedOTP, pFedMoAP).
Detailed cost analysis (Appendix E) showing pFedMMA communicates only the shared r×r projections (3,072 params/round) and achieves a favorable accuracy-communication trade-off versus baselines.

Thorough ablations on scaling factor, adapter dimension, starting layer, and sharing strategy, including a useful ablation showing that local-only adapters (no federation) degrade base/novel performance significantly (Table 18).

Results consistently show the best harmonic mean on the main 7-dataset benchmark (Table 1, e.g., HM 84.15 vs 79.09 for the next best), demonstrating the claimed personalization-generalization balance in the headline setting.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the adapter architecture is directly adopted from MMA (Yang et al., 2024), and the core federated contribution—keeping some modules local while averaging others—is essentially the well-established partial personalization paradigm (e.g., FedPer, PartialFed, Arivazhagan et al. 2019) applied to this adapter. The 'first adapter-based PFL for VLMs' claim is a first-mover claim rather than a deep methodological contribution; the method section contains essentially one equation.

No theoretical or analytical justification for why the shared projection (rather than up/down projections) should carry the generalization signal; the design rationale is intuitive but entirely post-hoc/empirical, and the asymmetric objective is not formally analyzed (no convergence or generalization guarantees).

Evidence of superiority is not uniform across settings: on ViT-B/32 (Tables 4, 8) several per-dataset deltas are negative (e.g., DTD HM −14.17%, OxfordPets −2.38% at 16 shots), and on Office-Caltech10 (Table 3) pFedMMA's average advantage over FedPGP is marginal (21.33 vs 20.71) with clear losses on Amazon (9.26 vs 20.34) and Webcam. The DomainNet jump (47.17 vs ~24.7) is striking but unexplained and inconsistent with the Office-Caltech results; some cells show 0.00 accuracy, raising setup questions.

Aggregation inconsistency and unclear protocol details: Algorithm 1 selects a subset St of clients but averages over all N clients; the paper does not clarify how base/novel evaluation is performed for personalized models (whether CLIP zero-shot is mixed in), which complicates interpreting novel-class gains; only mean accuracy over 3 seeds is reported, with no variance/significance analysis.

Typos and polish issues (e.g., 'Implimentation Details', 'lable shift'), and some baselines in the federated VLM adaptation space (e.g., FedCLIP, FedPETuning-style adapter baselines, or a simple FedAvg-over-adapters baseline matching pFedMMA's parameter count) are absent, making it harder to isolate whether gains come from the asymmetric aggregation or merely from the stronger MMA adapter capacity (248k trainable params vs ~8-16k for prompt baselines).

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: balancing personalization and generalization when adapting vision-language models in federated settings, and the adapter-based formulation is a reasonable alternative to the dominant prompt-tuning line of work.

The empirical coverage is broad: eleven datasets, two backbones (ViT-B/16 and ViT-B/32), five shot settings, ablations over scaling factor, adapter dimension, insertion layer, and sharing strategy, plus learning curves.

The communication cost analysis (Appendix E) is a nice addition, quantifying trainable parameters, per-round communication, training time, and memory alongside accuracy, which many comparable papers omit.
The method is clearly described (Eq. 2-3, Algorithm 1), and the asymmetric update (local up/down projections, globally aggregated shared projection) is simple and easy to reproduce in principle.
Ablation Table 18/13 provides evidence that sharing the low-rank subspace matters compared to a purely local variant.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially the centralized MMA adapter (Yang et al. 2024) transplanted into FL, combined with the long-established PFL idea of splitting parameters into shared vs. client-specific components (FedPer, PartialFed, LG-FedAvg, Collins et al., FedPerFix). The 'asymmetric aggregation' is not new, and the paper does not identify or solve any FL-specific technical difficulty beyond this standard split.

The claim of being 'the first adapter-based approach for PFL of VLMs' is contradicted by the paper's own related work: FedCLIP (Lu et al.) is described as 'integrating attention-based adapters' in federated CLIP adaptation, and FedPerFix (Sun et al. 2023) does partial model personalization of ViTs in FL. Neither is compared against.

Unfair capacity comparison: pFedMMA trains 248,832 local parameters vs. 8,192-16,384 for all prompt-tuning baselines (Table 17), a ~15-30x larger local budget. The strong local accuracy may largely reflect this extra capacity rather than the proposed design; the paper does not control for trainable parameter count across methods.

Results do not consistently support the claims. In Table 3, pFedMMA's Office-Caltech10 average (21.33) is only marginally above FedPGP (20.71) with erratic per-domain results (9.26 on Amazon), and Table 10 contains a 0.00 accuracy entry, suggesting instability. In Table 4 (ViT-B/32), several HM deltas are negative, yet the text claims pFedMMA 'consistently achieves the best trade-off.' Absolute accuracies on Office-Caltech10 (~9-21% for a 10-class problem) appear implausibly low and are not discussed.
No variance reporting: Appendix C.2 states each experiment is repeated with three seeds, but no standard deviations or significance tests appear anywhere, despite several margins being within ~1%.

Missing important baselines: federated adapter/PEFT methods that directly compete with the proposal (FedPETuning, FedBABU, FedPerFix, FedPara) are cited but not evaluated; the comparison set is entirely prompt-based plus pFedMoAP.

Typos and polish issues ('Implimentation Details', 'lable shift', Eq. 3 notation inconsistencies, references with missing years/venues) reduce confidence in overall care; the Appendix D.3 text also mislabels Figure 3 vs Figure 5.

Some design justifications are post-hoc: the choice of a 32-dim shared layer over the better-performing 128-dim option is justified purely by parameter count, and different hyperparameters (alpha=0.005, different starting layers) appear to be selected per setting, raising concerns about tuning asymmetry between the proposed method and baselines.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: balancing personalization and generalization in personalized federated fine-tuning of VLMs, with a compelling observation (Fig. 1) that strong personalized prompt-tuning methods degrade badly on unseen classes.

Extensive empirical evaluation: eleven datasets covering label shift, feature shift, and pathological non-IID splits, two backbones (ViT-B/16, B/32), five shot settings, and three random seeds per experiment.

Comprehensive ablations on the scaling factor, adapter dimension, starting layer, and adapter-sharing strategy (Tables 5, 11-15, 18), including a useful ablation (Table 18) showing that globally synchronizing the shared subspace is necessary.

Detailed and transparent communication/computation cost analysis (Appendix E) showing a favorable accuracy-communication trade-off: only ~3K parameters communicated per round versus thousands locally.
Consistently strong harmonic-mean results across shots and datasets on the base-to-novel protocol (Tables 1, 7), the central metric for the personalization-generalization trade-off.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the adapter design is directly adopted from MMA (Yang et al. 2024), and the asymmetric local-update/global-aggregation scheme is a well-established partial-personalization pattern in PFL (FedPer, FedRep, PartialFed, local/representation decomposition lines of work). The contribution is essentially a combination of known components applied to a new setting, and no theoretical or principled justification is given for why the shared middle projection (rather than, e.g., the up-projections) is the right component to aggregate.

Suspicious baseline numbers raise evaluation-concerns: zero-shot CLIP is reported at ~10% accuracy on DomainNet and Office-Caltech10 (Tables 3, 9, 10), which is implausibly low for CLIP on these benchmarks (even with 10 selected classes, near-random performance suggests a protocol or evaluation mismatch). Since the large margins in Table 3 rest on these baselines, this must be verified.

Results are mixed in several settings: on Office-Caltech10 (Table 3) pFedMMA's advantage is marginal (21.33 vs 20.71) and it loses on two of four domains; Table 9 shows pFedMMA underperforming FedPGP in several β settings; Table 8 (ViT-B/32) shows substantial losses on DTD and SUN397, and ∆ rows are inconsistent/partially missing; Table 10 contains a 0.00 accuracy entry for one domain, suggesting training instability that is not discussed.

Missing adapter-based FL baselines: the paper claims to be 'the first adapter-based approach for PFL of VLMs' and cites FedCLIP (adapter-based FL), yet all learned baselines are prompt-based. A direct comparison against at least one adapter-based federated method is needed to support the architecture choice.

No standard deviations or significance tests are reported despite three repetitions, so small margins (e.g., +0.14% on CIFAR-10, +0.18% HM on Caltech101, several negative ∆ entries) cannot be assessed.
Hyperparameter sensitivity to α is extreme (HM ranges from 7.6 to 83.3 in Table 5), and baselines appear to use default configurations; fairness of tuning across methods is not discussed.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, and several protocol details (how base/novel class splits interact with the 10-client pathological partition, exactly which classes count as 'base' for a given client) are under-specified.
